title: The $24 Bag of Rice: How US Tariffs Are Reshaping the Desi Pantry
excerpt: With US duties on Indian goods at 50 percent, staples from Sona Masoori rice to filter coffee have surged in price — and Pakistani brands are quietly filling the gap.
body:
The twenty-pound bag of Sona Masoori rice that Raghav, a New Jersey resident, used to buy for sixteen dollars now costs twenty-four. His Cothas filter coffee, once seven dollars for a 450-gram tin, is eleven. Every dal variety on the shelf has climbed in the same proportion. Welcome to the desi pantry in the age of the fifty-percent tariff.

When the United States doubled its duties on Indian products to fifty percent in late August last year, the impact was immediate — but the real pain arrived a few months later, once grocery stores exhausted their pre-tariff inventory and restocked at the new landed cost. For the roughly five million Indian Americans who depend on imported staples that have no domestic substitute, the maths is brutal.

## The Price of a Thali

The Hindu BusinessLine surveyed Indian Americans across several states and found price escalations of five to fifteen percent on different grocery items. In California, Shekhar reported that the price of dosa at his local restaurant jumped from twenty to twenty-five dollars in just fifteen days. Priya, another respondent, said the cost of getting individual shipments from India — care packages of pickles, papads, and snacks that families send across — has doubled.

The tariff does not discriminate between luxury and necessity. Hing, the pungent asafoetida that anchors every South Indian tadka, is imported almost exclusively from India. So is jaggery, curry leaf paste, and dozens of masala blends whose recipes are proprietary to Indian manufacturers. These are not products a Costco house brand can replicate.

Even where substitutes exist, the cultural gap is wide. Indian Americans can buy generic long-grain rice, but Sona Masoori and specific aged basmati varieties carry flavour profiles and starch qualities that define regional dishes. Asking a Hyderabadi to make biryani with Jasmine rice is like asking a Neapolitan to make pizza with a flour tortilla — technically possible, culturally absurd.

## Pakistan Fills the Gap

The more consequential shift is happening on the supply side. Pakistan, which faces significantly lower US tariffs than India, is quietly capturing market share in categories where the two countries compete directly. Basmati rice is the clearest example. Pakistan is the world's second-largest basmati exporter after India, and its brands — Falak, Guard, Lal Qilla — are already staples in Middle Eastern and British markets. American importers who once defaulted to Indian basmati are now running the numbers on Pakistani alternatives that land at a materially lower cost.

According to a recent analysis by USISPF chief Mukesh Aghi, the tariff differential between India and Pakistan has become a central friction point in US-India trade negotiations. An initial framework would have brought Indian duties down to eighteen percent, giving Indian exporters a competitive edge. But shifts in the US tariff structure — including additional duties of ten to twelve-and-a-half percent on goods from countries the USTR has flagged over forced labour concerns — have complicated the picture.

For Indian grocery exporters, the arithmetic is existential. The US was the largest buyer of Indian spices in financial year 2025-26, importing $624 million worth despite reduced volumes — overtaking China, which sharply cut its purchases of chilli and cumin. But overall Indian spice exports fell 6.1 percent in value to $4.43 billion, a decline driven in part by the tariff headwinds from the American market.

## The Desi Kitchen Adapts

Indian Americans are adapting the way immigrant communities always have: by shopping smarter and cooking differently. Costco, which sells twenty-pound bags of Sona Masoori for twenty-one dollars, has become the de facto Indian grocery store for families who previously shopped exclusively at Patel Brothers or India Bazaar. Bulk buying clubs on WhatsApp and Facebook, where families in the same ZIP code pool orders to split shipping from India, have exploded in activity.

Some families are cooking less frequently with imported ingredients and stretching what they have. Others are substituting — using domestic chickpeas instead of imported chana dal, or switching to locally roasted coffee brands. A few are simply absorbing the cost, treating the tariff surcharge as a tax on identity.

## What Comes Next

The US and India are in advanced negotiations on a trade framework that could bring tariffs down meaningfully. President Trump has publicly signalled that a deal is close. But even if tariffs fall to the proposed eighteen percent, prices at the Indian grocery store will not snap back overnight. Importers who signed contracts at fifty-percent duty rates will need to cycle through existing inventory, and retailers who have already repriced their shelves have little incentive to cut back quickly.

For now, the twenty-four-dollar bag of rice sits on the shelf as a daily reminder that trade policy is not an abstraction. It is what a family in Edison, New Jersey, pays to eat the food that tastes like home.
